aws-saa-secure-cues.cue: An allow and a matching explicit deny both apply to the same request
aws-saa-secure-cues.detail: A matching explicit deny overrides any allow.

aws-saa-secure-cues.cue: Cap the maximum permissions of one IAM user or role inside this account
aws-saa-secure-cues.detail: A permissions boundary limits one identity. It does not grant a permission by itself.
aws-saa-secure-cues.hook: Boundary is a ceiling, not a grant.

aws-saa-secure-cues.cue: Limit what member accounts in the organization are allowed to do
aws-saa-secure-cues.detail: An SCP is a guardrail on accounts in the organization. It does not grant a permission by itself.
aws-saa-secure-cues.hook: SCP guards accounts, not one user.

aws-saa-secure-cues.cue: Workforce users should sign in through the company identity provider
aws-saa-secure-cues.detail: Federation lets the workforce use the company IdP instead of an IAM user password for each person.

aws-saa-secure-cues.cue: A person in account A must work in account B without a long-lived access key
aws-saa-secure-cues.detail: The target role trust allows the source principal, and the caller receives temporary credentials.
aws-saa-secure-cues.hook: Assume a role. Do not copy a key.

aws-saa-secure-cues.cue: Managed keys that AWS services can use to encrypt data
aws-saa-secure-cues.detail: KMS is the managed key service integrated with AWS encryption.
aws-saa-secure-cues.hook: AWS service encryption usually calls KMS.

aws-saa-secure-cues.cue: Dedicated hardware security modules that the customer controls
aws-saa-secure-cues.detail: CloudHSM is dedicated HSM hardware under customer control, not the shared KMS service.

aws-saa-secure-cues.cue: A TLS certificate for a supported AWS integration should be provisioned and renewed for that service
aws-saa-secure-cues.detail: ACM provisions and manages TLS certificates for supported AWS integrations. It is not a store for database passwords.
aws-saa-secure-cues.hook: Certificate for the load balancer, not the DB password.

aws-saa-secure-cues.cue: The object is encrypted, and a broad read permission still exists
aws-saa-secure-cues.answer: Encryption does not replace the read permission
aws-saa-secure-cues.detail: Key use and data access are separate. Encrypting data does not remove an overly broad read permission.
aws-saa-secure-cues.hook: Ciphertext still needs an allow to be denied.

aws-saa-resilient-cues.cue: One published message must reach many subscribers
aws-saa-resilient-cues.detail: SNS is pub/sub. A queue is for one consumer pipeline, not a fan-out by itself.

aws-saa-resilient-cues.cue: A rule should match events from AWS services and send them to targets
aws-saa-resilient-cues.detail: EventBridge routes events with rules. It is not the durable work queue.

aws-saa-resilient-cues.cue: A message that keeps failing should leave the main queue
aws-saa-resilient-cues.detail: A dead-letter queue holds messages that could not be processed, so one poison message does not block the rest.

aws-saa-resilient-cues.cue: The same standard-queue message may arrive more than once
aws-saa-resilient-cues.detail: SQS standard queues are at-least-once. The consumer must tolerate a duplicate.

aws-saa-resilient-cues.cue: Hide an in-flight SQS message until the consumer finishes or the timeout ends
aws-saa-resilient-cues.detail: Visibility timeout hides a received message. It does not delete it. The consumer still has to delete a success.

aws-saa-resilient-cues.cue: Session files on one instance make that instance hard to replace
aws-saa-resilient-cues.detail: Horizontal replacement needs state off the instance. Local session files tie the user to one machine.

aws-saa-resilient-cues.cue: Both sites serve production traffic, and either site can take the load
aws-saa-resilient-cues.detail: Active/active costs more and recovers faster than a standby that still has to scale up. There is no universal minute guarantee.

aws-saa-resilient-cues.cue: Recovery starts from backups after the failure, accepting the slowest of these patterns
aws-saa-resilient-cues.detail: Backup and restore is the lower-cost, slower-recovery end of the DR line. It is not a warm environment already running.

aws-saa-resilient-cues.cue: Every Application Load Balancer target is unhealthy
aws-saa-resilient-cues.answer: ALB fail-open sends traffic to all targets
aws-saa-resilient-cues.detail: When no target is healthy, an ALB fails open and sends requests to all targets. A health check is not a universal stop.

aws-saa-performance-cues.cue: Persistent block storage that remains available after the instance stops
aws-saa-performance-cues.detail: EBS is persistent block storage in one Availability Zone. Stopping the instance does not delete the volume by itself.
aws-saa-performance-cues.hook: Stop the instance, the volume remains.

aws-saa-performance-cues.cue: Temporary block storage that can be lost when the instance stops
aws-saa-performance-cues.detail: Instance store is scratch storage tied to the host. It is not a durable volume for data you must keep.
aws-saa-performance-cues.hook: Scratch disk. Do not keep the only copy there.

aws-saa-performance-cues.cue: Many clients need key-addressed object storage, not a file system mount
aws-saa-performance-cues.detail: S3 stores objects by key. It is not a replacement for a POSIX file system or a block volume.
aws-saa-performance-cues.hook: Bucket and key, not a drive letter.

aws-saa-performance-cues.cue: The same stateless work should run on more instances
aws-saa-performance-cues.detail: Horizontal scaling adds instances. The work has to be partitionable. A bigger single instance is vertical scaling.
aws-saa-performance-cues.hook: More machines, not a bigger one.

aws-saa-performance-cues.cue: Too many Lambda executions are running at the same time for this account
aws-saa-performance-cues.detail: Lambda concurrency is the number of executions in flight. Extra invocations are throttled when the limit is reached.
aws-saa-performance-cues.hook: In flight, not requests per day.

aws-saa-performance-cues.cue: Scale relational reads and accept that the replica can lag
aws-saa-performance-cues.detail: A read replica adds read capacity and can lag. It is not the automatic failover of a Multi-AZ standby.
aws-saa-performance-cues.hook: Reads scale. Writes and failover do not.

aws-saa-performance-cues.cue: Many short-lived application connections are exhausting the database
aws-saa-performance-cues.detail: RDS Proxy pools connections for supported engines. It does not make an incompatible query faster.

aws-saa-performance-cues.cue: Stream order is required only for records that share a partition key
aws-saa-performance-cues.detail: Kinesis ordering follows the shard and partition key. The whole stream is not one ordered line.

aws-saa-performance-cues.cue: Discover the schema and transform data before it is queried in the lake
aws-saa-performance-cues.detail: Glue catalogs and transforms data. It is not the service that fans out one notification to subscribers.

aws-saa-cost-cues.cue: Reads are infrequent and immediate, and the object must survive loss of an Availability Zone
aws-saa-cost-cues.detail: Standard-IA keeps infrequently accessed objects across Availability Zones with immediate retrieval.

aws-saa-cost-cues.cue: The infrequent object can be recreated, and loss of one Availability Zone is acceptable
aws-saa-cost-cues.detail: One Zone-IA stores the object in a single Availability Zone at a lower price than Standard-IA.
aws-saa-cost-cues.hook: One zone, recreate if it is lost.

aws-saa-cost-cues.cue: An EBS volume is no longer attached and is still billed
aws-saa-cost-cues.answer: Delete the unused volume after checking it
aws-saa-cost-cues.detail: An unattached EBS volume still incurs storage charges. Delete it only when the data is no longer required.

aws-saa-cost-cues.cue: Many tiny objects are moving to an infrequent class because the per-GB price looks lower
aws-saa-cost-cues.answer: Check the infrequent-class minimum size and duration
aws-saa-cost-cues.detail: A lower per-GB price can cost more when minimum object size, minimum duration, and request charges apply.
aws-saa-cost-cues.hook: The GB price is not the whole bill.

aws-saa-cost-cues.cue: A steady daily baseline and separate peaks that can be interrupted
aws-saa-cost-cues.answer: Commit the baseline and use Spot for the peaks
aws-saa-cost-cues.detail: A commitment fits measured steady use. Spot fits work that can stop and restart. Spot is not a capacity guarantee.
aws-saa-cost-cues.hook: Commit the floor. Spot the burst.

aws-saa-cost-cues.cue: The work cannot stop, and there is no measured commitment to buy yet
aws-saa-cost-cues.detail: On-Demand has no term and is not interrupted for capacity. It is the flexible price, not the committed discount.

aws-saa-cost-cues.cue: The database looks expensive, and nobody has measured the actual queries
aws-saa-cost-cues.answer: Measure the database before buying a larger instance
aws-saa-cost-cues.detail: A larger instance is not justified by the price list alone. Measure connections, CPU, and query shape first.

aws-saa-cost-cues.cue: A cache would remove repeated reads, and the comparison ignores the cache price
aws-saa-cost-cues.answer: Include the cache in the database bill
aws-saa-cost-cues.detail: A cache can cut database load, but the comparison has to include the cache nodes and the freshness the workload allows.
aws-saa-cost-cues.hook: The cache is part of the bill.

aws-saa-cost-cues.cue: Private S3 traffic should leave the NAT path without an hourly endpoint fee
aws-saa-cost-cues.answer: S3 gateway endpoint rather than an interface endpoint
aws-saa-cost-cues.detail: A gateway endpoint is a route-table target for S3 or DynamoDB and has no hourly fee. An interface endpoint adds hourly and data-processing charges.
aws-saa-cost-cues.hook: S3 route-table endpoint has no hourly fee.

aws-saa-service-compare.scenario: Linux instances need a shared file system
aws-saa-service-compare.detail: EFS is a shared file system for Linux workloads. It is not block storage for one instance.

aws-saa-service-compare.scenario: Windows instances need a shared SMB file system
aws-saa-service-compare.answer: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
aws-saa-service-compare.detail: FSx for Windows File Server provides managed Windows file shares. EFS is the Linux shared file system.

aws-saa-service-compare.scenario: Run a container task without managing EC2 instances
aws-saa-service-compare.detail: Fargate is serverless compute for supported container tasks. ECS and EKS can also run on EC2 instances you manage.

aws-saa-service-compare.scenario: A key-value workload needs single-digit millisecond reads at a changing request rate
aws-saa-service-compare.detail: DynamoDB is a managed key-value and document database. A relational join-heavy schema is a different choice.

aws-saa-service-compare.scenario: Run SQL on objects in S3 without loading them into a database first
aws-saa-service-compare.detail: Athena queries data in S3. It does not replace a transactional database for the application.
aws-saa-service-compare.hook: SQL on the files in place.

whichTwo.prompt: Which TWO statements about access control are correct?
whichTwo.detail: Deny overrides allow. A boundary limits an identity and does not grant access.
whichTwo.hook: Deny wins. A boundary is a ceiling.

choices.text: A matching explicit deny overrides an allow
choices.why: IAM evaluation lets an explicit deny beat an allow.

choices.text: A permissions boundary sets a maximum on one IAM user or role and does not itself grant access
choices.why: The boundary filters identity-based allows. It is not an allow.

choices.text: A permissions boundary grants every action listed in it, even when the identity policy has no allow
choices.why: The boundary does not grant. The identity still needs an allow.

choices.text: A service control policy on one IAM user replaces that user's identity policy
choices.why: An SCP applies to accounts in the organization, not as a per-user identity policy.

whichTwo.prompt: Which TWO statements about network controls are correct?
whichTwo.detail: Security groups are stateful and attached to resources. NACLs are stateless and attached to subnets.
whichTwo.hook: Group remembers. NACL does not.

choices.text: A security group is stateful
choices.why: Return traffic for an allowed flow is allowed by the security group.

choices.text: A network ACL is stateless and is applied at the subnet
choices.why: A NACL evaluates each packet, including the return, and it is associated with a subnet.

choices.text: A security group can explicitly deny one source IP while allowing the rest of the traffic
choices.why: Security group rules are allows. A NACL is the control with explicit deny.

choices.text: A network ACL remembers the outbound packet and automatically allows the return
choices.why: NACLs are stateless, so the return direction needs its own rule.

whichTwo.prompt: Which TWO statements about edge protection are correct?
whichTwo.detail: WAF filters web requests. Shield is DDoS protection. They are not substitutes.
whichTwo.hook: WAF reads the request. Shield absorbs the flood.

choices.text: AWS WAF filters HTTP and HTTPS requests by rules you define
choices.why: WAF inspects web requests and can block patterns such as SQL injection.

choices.text: AWS Shield is the managed DDoS protection service
choices.why: Shield addresses DDoS. It is not the web request filter.

choices.text: AWS WAF is the service that stops a volumetric network flood by itself
choices.why: A volumetric flood is a DDoS problem for Shield, not a WAF rule match.

choices.text: AWS Shield inspects SQL strings inside an HTTP body and blocks the injection
choices.why: SQL-injection filtering is a WAF rule, not Shield's job.

whichTwo.prompt: Which TWO statements about keys and secrets are correct?
whichTwo.detail: KMS manages keys. Secrets Manager stores and can rotate the secret value.
whichTwo.hook: Key service versus secret value.

choices.text: AWS KMS manages cryptographic keys used by AWS encryption integrations
choices.why: KMS is the key-management service, not the password vault.

choices.text: Secrets Manager stores and can rotate a database credential
choices.why: The secret value and its rotation live in Secrets Manager.

choices.text: Storing a password in KMS is the rotation feature for database credentials
choices.why: KMS holds keys. Rotation of the database secret is Secrets Manager.

choices.text: Encrypting an object removes the need for an IAM allow on GetObject
choices.why: Encryption and the read permission are separate checks.

whichTwo.prompt: Which TWO statements about private service access are correct?
whichTwo.detail: A VPC endpoint keeps supported service traffic off the public internet path. It is not a NAT gateway.
whichTwo.hook: Private path to the service.

choices.text: A gateway endpoint for S3 is a route in the route table
choices.why: S3 and DynamoDB gateway endpoints are route-table targets.

choices.text: An interface endpoint is an elastic network interface in the subnet
choices.why: Interface endpoints use PrivateLink network interfaces.

choices.text: A NAT gateway is the private path from the VPC to S3 that avoids the internet
choices.why: A public NAT gateway sends IPv4 to the internet through an internet gateway.

choices.text: A gateway endpoint for S3 has the same hourly charge as an interface endpoint
choices.why: The S3 gateway endpoint has no hourly fee. Interface endpoints do.

whichTwo.prompt: Which TWO statements about workload identity are correct?
whichTwo.detail: Roles and federation issue temporary credentials. A copied access key is a long-lived secret.
whichTwo.hook: Temporary credentials for the workload.

choices.text: An IAM role can provide temporary credentials to a workload
choices.why: The application assumes a role instead of embedding a long-lived key.

choices.text: Federation can give a workforce user temporary credentials from the company identity provider
choices.why: The IdP session becomes a temporary AWS session.

choices.text: The recommended workload credential is a long-lived access key in the source repository
choices.why: A key in source is a lasting secret. Use a role.

choices.text: The AWS account root user should be the daily credential for the application
choices.why: Root is not an application identity.

whichTwo.prompt: Which TWO statements about decoupling are correct?
whichTwo.detail: SQS buffers work and can deliver a message more than once. SNS fans out.
whichTwo.hook: Queue buffers. Topic notifies.

choices.text: SQS lets the producer continue when consumers are briefly slower
choices.why: The queue holds the work between the two sides.

choices.text: A standard SQS queue can deliver the same message more than once
choices.why: Standard queues are at-least-once, so the consumer must be idempotent.

choices.text: SNS is the durable buffer that hides work until one consumer polls it
choices.why: SNS delivers to subscribers. The durable poll buffer is SQS.

choices.text: A standard queue guarantees that each message is delivered exactly once in order
choices.why: Exactly-once ordered delivery is not the standard-queue contract.

whichTwo.prompt: Which TWO statements about recovery patterns are correct?
whichTwo.detail: Pilot light keeps a core running. Warm standby is a reduced live environment. Neither is a fixed number of minutes.
whichTwo.hook: Relative cost and speed, not a minute promise.

choices.text: Pilot light keeps the core of the recovery environment running and scales the rest during recovery
choices.why: The core stays up. Full capacity is added when you fail over.

choices.text: Warm standby runs a reduced but functional copy that you scale during recovery
choices.why: Warm standby is already serving at lower capacity.

choices.text: Backup and restore keeps a full second site serving production traffic
choices.why: Backup and restore recovers from backups after the failure. It is not an already-serving second site.

choices.text: These patterns guarantee recovery in a fixed number of minutes for every workload
choices.why: The patterns are relative. The actual time depends on the workload and the test.

whichTwo.prompt: Which TWO statements about recovery objectives are correct?
whichTwo.detail: RTO is time to recover. RPO is how much data you can lose.
whichTwo.hook: T is time. P is the point in the data.

choices.text: RTO is the maximum acceptable time to restore service
choices.why: Recovery time is how long the service may stay down.

choices.text: RPO is the maximum acceptable data-loss window
choices.why: Recovery point is how far back the restored data may be.

choices.text: RPO is the maximum time the application may stay unavailable
choices.why: Downtime length is RTO, not RPO.

choices.text: RTO is the number of transactions you can afford to lose
choices.why: Lost data is the recovery point, not the recovery time.

whichTwo.prompt: Which TWO statements about RDS availability are correct?
whichTwo.detail: A single-standby Multi-AZ instance fails over and the standby is not a read endpoint. A read replica scales reads.
whichTwo.hook: Standby fails over. Replica serves reads.

choices.text: Multi-AZ with one standby fails over when the primary Availability Zone is lost
choices.why: The standby exists for failover of that deployment type.

choices.text: A read replica can serve read queries and can lag behind the writer
choices.why: Replicas add read capacity. Replication is asynchronous, so lag is possible.

choices.text: The single Multi-AZ standby is a general-purpose read endpoint
choices.why: That standby is for failover, not for application reads. A readable standby is a different deployment.

choices.text: A read replica is the automatic same-Region failover target of a single-standby Multi-AZ instance
choices.why: Failover uses the standby. A read replica is a separate read-scaling feature.

whichTwo.prompt: Which TWO statements about load-balancer health are correct?
whichTwo.detail: Health checks remove bad targets. If every target is unhealthy, an ALB fails open.
whichTwo.hook: Some unhealthy: skip them. All unhealthy: fail open.

choices.text: Healthy targets receive traffic and unhealthy targets are taken out of rotation
choices.why: That is the normal health-check result.

choices.text: If every ALB target is unhealthy, the load balancer sends requests to the targets anyway
choices.why: The ALB fails open when the target group has no healthy target.

choices.text: An unhealthy target stays in rotation because the health check is only a metric
choices.why: A failed health check removes the target while any healthy target remains.

choices.text: An ALB stops all traffic forever once one target fails a health check
choices.why: One failure removes that target. The healthy targets still receive traffic.

whichTwo.prompt: Which TWO statements about replacing instances are correct?
whichTwo.detail: Local session state blocks replacement. A queue lets the other side slow down without losing the request.
whichTwo.hook: No local session. Queue the burst.

choices.text: Session files stored only on the instance tie the user to that instance
choices.why: Replacing the instance loses or strands that session.

choices.text: A queue absorbs a burst so the producer does not have to wait for every consumer
choices.why: The queue is the buffer between the two rates.

choices.text: Keeping the shopping cart on the instance disk is what makes horizontal replacement safe
choices.why: Local disk state makes replacement unsafe for that user.

choices.text: EventBridge stores the work until a worker polls and deletes it
choices.why: That poll-and-delete buffer is SQS. EventBridge routes events.

whichTwo.prompt: Which TWO statements about storage durability are correct?
whichTwo.detail: EBS persists across stop. Instance store can be lost on stop.
whichTwo.hook: EBS stays. Instance store may not.

choices.text: An EBS volume remains available after the instance stops, unless you delete it
choices.why: EBS is persistent block storage, separate from the instance lifetime.

choices.text: Instance-store data can be lost when the instance stops or the host fails
choices.why: Instance store is temporary storage on the host.

choices.text: Instance store is the durable place for the only copy of a database
choices.why: Instance store is scratch storage. Do not keep the only copy there.

choices.text: Stopping an instance always deletes its EBS volumes
choices.why: Stop does not delete EBS volumes. DeleteOnTermination is a separate setting, and it applies on termination.

whichTwo.prompt: Which TWO statements about shared files are correct?
whichTwo.detail: EFS is the Linux shared file system. FSx for Windows serves SMB.
whichTwo.hook: Linux EFS. Windows FSx.

choices.text: Amazon EFS provides a shared file system for Linux clients
choices.why: EFS is the elastic Linux file system.

choices.text: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server provides managed Windows file shares
choices.why: Windows SMB shares are the FSx for Windows use, not EFS.

choices.text: Amazon EFS is the managed SMB file server for Windows instances
choices.why: EFS is not the Windows SMB product. That role is FSx for Windows.

choices.text: Amazon S3 is a POSIX file system you mount as the only disk of an instance
choices.why: S3 is object storage addressed by key, not the instance's block disk.

whichTwo.prompt: Which TWO statements about compute scaling are correct?
whichTwo.detail: Horizontal scaling adds instances and needs stateless work. A larger instance is vertical scaling.
whichTwo.hook: Out is more machines. Up is a bigger machine.

choices.text: Horizontal scaling adds instances and needs work that can be split
choices.why: More instances help only when the work is not pinned to one machine.

choices.text: Vertical scaling changes the size of an instance and keeps that instance as the failure boundary
choices.why: A bigger instance is still one instance.

choices.text: Horizontal scaling is choosing a larger instance type for the same one machine
choices.why: A larger type is vertical scaling.

choices.text: Fargate requires you to patch the EC2 instances that run the task
choices.why: Fargate runs the task without an EC2 fleet for you to patch.

whichTwo.prompt: Which TWO statements about database reads are correct?
whichTwo.detail: Replicas can lag. RDS Proxy pools connections. Neither one is a cache of DynamoDB.
whichTwo.hook: Replica lag. Proxy pools.

choices.text: A read replica can be behind the writer
choices.why: Replication to a read replica is asynchronous.

choices.text: RDS Proxy pools database connections for supported engines
choices.why: The proxy sits between the app and the database and reuses connections.

choices.text: A read replica is always a strongly consistent view of the latest commit
choices.why: The replica can lag, so a just-written row may be missing.

choices.text: DAX makes every DynamoDB read strongly consistent and served from cache
choices.why: DAX serves eventually consistent cache hits. Strongly consistent reads go to DynamoDB.

whichTwo.prompt: Which TWO statements about streaming are correct?
whichTwo.detail: Data Streams is for your consumers. Firehose delivers to a destination. Order is per shard.
whichTwo.hook: Consumers read the stream. Firehose delivers it.

choices.text: Kinesis Data Streams holds records for applications that read them
choices.why: Your consumers read and checkpoint the stream.

choices.text: Data Firehose can deliver a stream to S3 without you running the consumer
choices.why: Firehose is managed delivery to supported destinations.

choices.text: Kinesis order is one sequence for every record in the stream, regardless of key
choices.why: Order follows the shard and partition key, not the entire stream.

choices.text: Athena stores the transactional rows of the application database
choices.why: Athena queries data in place, typically in S3. It is not the transactional store.

whichTwo.prompt: Which TWO statements about global entry points are correct?
whichTwo.detail: CloudFront caches content. Global Accelerator improves the network path to regional endpoints and does not cache the object.
whichTwo.hook: CloudFront caches. Accelerator routes.

choices.text: CloudFront can cache content at edge locations
choices.why: CloudFront is the CDN. Cache hits avoid a repeat trip to the origin.

choices.text: Global Accelerator sends TCP or UDP traffic onto the AWS network toward regional endpoints
choices.why: Accelerator is a network path, not an object cache.

choices.text: Global Accelerator caches HTML and images the way a CDN does
choices.why: Caching objects is CloudFront. Accelerator does not replace that cache.

choices.text: CloudFront is the dedicated private circuit from a data center to a VPC
choices.why: A dedicated private circuit is Direct Connect, not CloudFront.

whichTwo.prompt: Which TWO statements about infrequent S3 classes are correct?
whichTwo.detail: Standard-IA is multi-AZ. One Zone-IA is one zone and is for data you can recreate.
whichTwo.hook: IA still has zones. One Zone is one zone.

choices.text: Standard-IA stores infrequently accessed objects across Availability Zones
choices.why: Standard-IA is the multi-AZ infrequent class with immediate retrieval.

choices.text: One Zone-IA stores the object in a single Availability Zone
choices.why: Loss of that zone can lose the object, which is acceptable only if you can recreate it.

choices.text: One Zone-IA keeps a copy in every Availability Zone of the Region
choices.why: One Zone-IA is one zone. Multi-AZ infrequent storage is Standard-IA.

choices.text: Standard-IA is the class for data that must not be readable for hours
choices.why: Standard-IA retrieval is immediate. Long retrieval waits belong to Glacier classes, and those waits are not a single number for every option.

whichTwo.prompt: Which TWO statements about compute purchasing are correct?
whichTwo.detail: Spot can be interrupted. On-Demand is not interrupted for capacity and has no term.
whichTwo.hook: Spot can stop. On-Demand does not.

choices.text: Spot uses spare capacity and the instance can be interrupted
choices.why: Spot is for work that can stop and restart. It is not a capacity promise.

choices.text: On-Demand has no term commitment and is not taken back for capacity
choices.why: On-Demand is the flexible price for work that cannot be interrupted.

choices.text: Spot is a guarantee that the instance runs until you stop it
choices.why: Spot can be interrupted when AWS needs the capacity.

choices.text: A Savings Plan is the right commitment when you have not measured any steady usage
choices.why: A commitment needs a measured baseline. Unmeasured, uninterruptible work starts on On-Demand.

whichTwo.prompt: Which TWO statements about S3 network cost are correct?
whichTwo.detail: The S3 gateway endpoint has no hourly fee. An interface endpoint adds hourly and data-processing charges.
whichTwo.hook: Gateway for S3 has no hourly fee.

choices.text: An S3 gateway endpoint does not add an hourly endpoint fee
choices.why: The gateway endpoint is a route-table target without that hourly charge.

choices.text: An interface endpoint can charge hourly and for data processed
choices.why: Interface endpoints are elastic network interfaces with those charges.

choices.text: Sending S3 traffic through a NAT gateway is required for a private S3 path
choices.why: A gateway endpoint removes eligible S3 traffic from the NAT path.

choices.text: An S3 gateway endpoint and an interface endpoint have the same hourly price
choices.why: The gateway endpoint has no hourly fee. The interface endpoint does.

whichTwo.prompt: Which TWO statements about database cost are correct?
whichTwo.detail: Measure before a larger instance. A cache has its own price.
whichTwo.hook: Measure first. Count the cache.

choices.text: A larger database instance should follow a measurement, not only a price-list guess
choices.why: CPU, connections, and query shape decide whether a larger instance helps.

choices.text: A cache that removes repeated reads still belongs in the cost comparison
choices.why: The cache nodes are part of the bill.

choices.text: The lowest instance price is a reason to pick a database engine that cannot run the queries
choices.why: An incompatible engine does not meet the requirement, so its price is not the decision.

choices.text: Deleting backups is free of consequence when the recovery policy still requires them
choices.why: Backup retention is a recovery requirement. Removing it to save money breaks that requirement.

whichTwo.prompt: Which TWO statements about storage waste are correct?
whichTwo.detail: Unattached EBS is still billed. A lower per-GB class can cost more for tiny objects.
whichTwo.hook: Detached still bills. Tiny objects have a minimum.

choices.text: An unattached EBS volume can still incur storage charges
choices.why: Detaching the volume does not stop its storage charge.

choices.text: Infrequent-access classes can bill a minimum object size and a minimum duration
choices.why: The headline per-GB price is not the whole charge for a small or short-lived object.

choices.text: Detaching an EBS volume stops all charges for that volume
choices.why: The volume remains billable storage until you delete it.

choices.text: Moving every small object to an infrequent class always lowers the bill
choices.why: Minimum size, duration, and request charges can make the move more expensive.

whichTwo.prompt: Which TWO statements about commitments are correct?
whichTwo.detail: A commitment fits a measured baseline. A discount is not spare capacity and it is not a capacity guarantee.
whichTwo.hook: Commit what you measured. Spot what can stop.

choices.text: Savings Plans or eligible Reserved pricing fit a steady measured baseline
choices.why: The discount follows usage you expect to keep running.

choices.text: Interruption-tolerant peaks can use Spot while the baseline stays committed
choices.why: The two purchasing options solve different parts of the same workload.

choices.text: A Reserved discount promises that Spot capacity will be available
choices.why: A commitment discount and Spot spare capacity are different. Spot can be unavailable or interrupted.

choices.text: Rightsizing is unnecessary once a Savings Plan is active
choices.why: A commitment on an oversized resource still pays for capacity you do not use.

spotWrong.detail: A permissions boundary does not grant access. The other three statements match the evaluation and network models.
spotWrong.hook: The boundary is not an allow.

choices.text: A permissions boundary grants every action it lists, even with no identity-policy allow
choices.why: This is wrong. The boundary sets a maximum. It does not grant.

choices.text: A matching explicit deny overrides an allow
choices.why: This is true. Explicit deny wins the evaluation.

choices.text: A security group is stateful
choices.why: This is true. Allowed flows get their return traffic.

choices.text: An SCP limits accounts in the organization and does not by itself grant a permission
choices.why: This is true. An SCP is a guardrail, not an allow.

spotWrong.detail: NACLs are stateless. The other statements match the security group, WAF, and Shield roles.

choices.text: A network ACL remembers an allowed outbound connection and allows the return automatically
choices.why: This is wrong. A NACL is stateless, so the return needs a rule.

choices.text: A security group allows return traffic for a flow it allowed
choices.why: This is true. Security groups are stateful.

choices.text: AWS WAF can block a web request that matches a SQL-injection rule
choices.why: This is true. WAF filters the HTTP request.

choices.text: AWS Shield is for DDoS protection, not for SQL-injection rules
choices.why: This is true. Injection rules belong to WAF.

spotWrong.detail: The root user is not the application credential. Roles, federation, and deny behavior are the correct statements.

choices.text: The application should use the account root user for its daily AWS calls
choices.why: This is wrong. A workload uses a role and temporary credentials.

choices.text: An IAM role can hand a workload temporary credentials
choices.why: This is true. AssumeRole yields temporary credentials.

choices.text: Workforce access can be federated from a company identity provider
choices.why: This is true. Federation avoids an IAM user for every person.

choices.text: An explicit deny still applies when another policy allows the action
choices.why: This is true. The deny wins.

spotWrong.detail: KMS does not rotate the database password. Secrets Manager does. The other statements match KMS, CloudHSM, and ACM.
spotWrong.hook: Passwords are secrets, not KMS keys.

choices.text: AWS KMS rotates the database username and password on a schedule
choices.why: This is wrong. Credential rotation is Secrets Manager. KMS manages keys.

choices.text: AWS KMS manages keys that AWS services use for encryption
choices.why: This is true. KMS is the managed key service.

choices.text: CloudHSM is dedicated HSM hardware under customer control
choices.why: This is true. It is not the shared KMS service.

choices.text: ACM provisions TLS certificates for supported AWS integrations
choices.why: This is true. ACM is the certificate service, not the secret vault.

spotWrong.detail: Encryption does not delete a read permission. Macie, Secrets Manager, and private endpoints are described correctly.
spotWrong.hook: Encrypted is not the same as unauthorized.

choices.text: Encrypting an S3 object deletes every IAM allow for reading that object
choices.why: This is wrong. The read permission and the key permission are separate.

choices.text: Macie looks for sensitive data in Amazon S3
choices.why: This is true. Macie's focus is sensitive data in S3.

choices.text: Secrets Manager can store a database credential and rotate it
choices.why: This is true. That is the secret-value service.

choices.text: A VPC endpoint can keep supported AWS service traffic off the public internet
choices.why: This is true. The endpoint is a private path to the service.

spotWrong.detail: A NAT gateway is not the private S3 path. Shield, WAF, and security-group state are described correctly.
spotWrong.hook: NAT is internet egress, not the S3 endpoint.

choices.text: A public NAT gateway is the private, non-internet path from a VPC to S3
choices.why: This is wrong. Public NAT sends IPv4 through an internet gateway. The private S3 path is a gateway endpoint.

choices.text: AWS Shield provides managed DDoS protection
choices.why: This is true. Shield is the DDoS service.

choices.text: AWS WAF filters web requests
choices.why: This is true. WAF sees the HTTP request.

choices.text: Security groups do not require a separate rule for the return traffic of an allowed flow
choices.why: This is true because the group is stateful.

spotWrong.detail: Standard SQS is not exactly-once. SNS, EventBridge, and dead-letter queues are described correctly.
spotWrong.hook: Standard queue means at least once.

choices.text: A standard SQS queue delivers each message exactly once and in send order
choices.why: This is wrong. Standard queues are at-least-once with best-effort ordering.

choices.text: Amazon SNS publishes one message to many subscribers
choices.why: This is true. SNS is the fan-out.

choices.text: EventBridge rules route matching events to targets
choices.why: This is true. Rules select events and targets.

choices.text: A dead-letter queue can hold messages that failed processing
choices.why: This is true. The failed message leaves the main processing path.

spotWrong.detail: Visibility timeout hides a message. It does not delete it. The other three recovery and queue statements are correct.

choices.text: The visibility timeout deletes the SQS message as soon as a consumer receives it
choices.why: This is wrong. The timeout only hides the message. The consumer deletes it after success.

choices.text: RTO is how long the service may take to recover
choices.why: This is true. RTO is the time objective.

choices.text: RPO is how much recent data the recovery may lose
choices.why: This is true. RPO is the data-loss window.

choices.text: A queue lets a fast producer outrun a slower consumer without dropping the handoff
choices.why: This is true. The queue is the buffer.

spotWrong.detail: Backup and restore does not keep a second site serving. Pilot light, warm standby, and active/active are described by their relative roles.
spotWrong.hook: Backups are not a live second site.

choices.text: Backup and restore keeps a full second site serving users during normal operation
choices.why: This is wrong. That live second site is active/active or a scaled standby, not backup and restore.

choices.text: Pilot light keeps a core running and scales the rest at failover
choices.why: This is true. Only the core stays on.

choices.text: Warm standby is a reduced environment that is already running
choices.why: This is true. You scale it up during recovery.

choices.text: Active/active serves from more than one site
choices.why: This is true. Both sites take traffic.

spotWrong.detail: A read replica is not the single-standby failover mechanism. Multi-AZ failover, ALB fail-open, and externalized state are described correctly.

choices.text: An RDS read replica is the automatic failover target of a single-standby Multi-AZ instance
choices.why: This is wrong. Failover uses the standby. The replica is for reads and can lag.

choices.text: A single-standby Multi-AZ deployment fails over to the standby
choices.why: This is true for that deployment type.

choices.text: An ALB with no healthy targets fails open and sends requests to the registered targets
choices.why: This is true. Fail-open is the all-unhealthy behavior.

choices.text: Session state kept only on one instance makes that instance hard to replace
choices.why: This is true. The session has to move off the instance.

spotWrong.detail: The DR line has no universal minute guarantee. SNS, idempotent consumers, and Multi-AZ are described correctly.

choices.text: Pilot light, warm standby, and active/active each guarantee the same recovery time in minutes
choices.why: This is wrong. They are relative tradeoffs. The minutes come from a test of that workload.

choices.text: SNS delivers one notification to many subscribers
choices.why: This is true. That is pub/sub.

choices.text: A consumer of a standard queue should tolerate a duplicate message
choices.why: This is true. Delivery is at-least-once.

choices.text: Spreading a tier across Availability Zones survives loss of one zone
choices.why: This is true when the surviving zones still have capacity.

spotWrong.detail: EventBridge does not replace the SQS buffer. Dead-letter queues, warm standby, and RPO are described correctly.

choices.text: EventBridge is the polled queue that hides a message until the worker deletes it
choices.why: This is wrong. That behavior is SQS. EventBridge routes events with rules.

choices.text: A dead-letter queue keeps a poison message from blocking the main queue
choices.why: This is true. The failed message is set aside.

choices.text: Warm standby is already running at lower capacity
choices.why: This is true. You scale it during recovery.

choices.text: RPO describes lost data, not hours of downtime
choices.why: This is true. Downtime is RTO.

spotWrong.detail: Instance store is not durable database storage. EBS, S3, and EFS are described correctly.
spotWrong.hook: Scratch disk is not the database.

choices.text: Instance store is the durable disk for the only copy of a database
choices.why: This is wrong. Instance store can disappear on stop or host loss.

choices.text: EBS volume data remains after the instance stops
choices.why: This is true. EBS is persistent block storage.

choices.text: S3 addresses objects by key
choices.why: This is true. Clients use the bucket and key.

choices.text: EFS is a shared file system for Linux
choices.why: This is true. Linux clients share the file system.

spotWrong.detail: DAX does not serve strongly consistent reads from cache. Read replicas, RDS Proxy, and Fargate are described correctly.
spotWrong.hook: Strong reads skip the DAX cache.

choices.text: DAX serves strongly consistent DynamoDB reads from the cache
choices.why: This is wrong. Strongly consistent reads pass through to DynamoDB. Cache hits are eventually consistent.

choices.text: A read replica can lag behind the writer
choices.why: This is true. Replica reads are not a latest-commit guarantee.

choices.text: RDS Proxy pools connections for supported database engines
choices.why: This is true. The proxy reuses connections.

choices.text: Fargate runs a container without an EC2 fleet you manage
choices.why: This is true. You do not patch those instances.

spotWrong.detail: Global Accelerator does not cache objects. CloudFront, Direct Connect, and horizontal scaling are described correctly.
spotWrong.hook: Accelerator is a path, not a cache.

choices.text: Global Accelerator caches images and HTML at edge locations
choices.why: This is wrong. Object caching is CloudFront. Accelerator improves the network path.

choices.text: CloudFront can answer a repeated request from cache
choices.why: This is true when the object is cached and still fresh.

choices.text: Direct Connect is a dedicated private connection from on-premises to AWS
choices.why: This is true. It is not the CDN.

choices.text: Horizontal scaling adds instances rather than only enlarging one instance
choices.why: This is true. Enlarging one instance is vertical scaling.

spotWrong.detail: Kinesis does not order the entire stream as one line. Firehose, Glue, and Athena are described correctly.

choices.text: Kinesis Data Streams keeps one send order for every record in the stream
choices.why: This is wrong. Order is within a shard for a partition key.

choices.text: Data Firehose can deliver streaming data to S3
choices.why: This is true. Firehose is managed delivery.

choices.text: AWS Glue can catalog and transform data for analytics
choices.why: This is true. Glue is the catalog and transform service.

choices.text: Athena can query data in S3 with SQL
choices.why: This is true. The data stays in S3.

spotWrong.detail: S3 is not the block volume. Lambda concurrency, EBS, and FSx for Windows are described correctly.

choices.text: Amazon S3 is the block volume attached as the instance's boot disk
choices.why: This is wrong. The boot disk is EBS or instance store. S3 is object storage.

choices.text: Lambda concurrency counts executions in flight
choices.why: This is true. Hitting the limit throttles more invocations.

choices.text: An EBS volume is persistent block storage in one Availability Zone
choices.why: This is true. The volume stays in its zone.

choices.text: FSx for Windows File Server serves Windows file shares
choices.why: This is true. It is the Windows SMB file system.

spotWrong.detail: A larger instance is vertical scaling, not horizontal. RDS Proxy, shard order, and CloudFront are described correctly.

choices.text: Changing to a larger instance type is horizontal scaling
choices.why: This is wrong. A larger type is vertical scaling. Horizontal scaling adds instances.

choices.text: RDS Proxy is a connection pool, not a query cache
choices.why: This is true. It multiplexes connections to the database.

choices.text: Records that share a Kinesis partition key are ordered within that shard
choices.why: This is true. Other keys can be on other shards.

choices.text: CloudFront cache hits can avoid repeating the same origin fetch
choices.why: This is true when the cached object is still valid.

spotWrong.detail: Spot is not a run-until-you-stop guarantee. On-Demand, Standard-IA, and the gateway endpoint fee are described correctly.

choices.text: A Spot instance keeps running until you stop it, because the discount includes a capacity guarantee
choices.why: This is wrong. Spot uses spare capacity and can be interrupted.

choices.text: On-Demand is not interrupted to reclaim capacity
choices.why: This is true. On-Demand has no Spot interruption.

choices.text: Standard-IA keeps an infrequently accessed object in more than one Availability Zone
choices.why: This is true. One Zone-IA is the single-zone class.

choices.text: An S3 gateway endpoint does not add an hourly endpoint charge
choices.why: This is true. The hourly and data-processing charges belong to interface endpoints.

spotWrong.detail: One Zone-IA is not multi-AZ. Unused EBS, minimum charges, and measuring a database are described correctly.

choices.text: S3 One Zone-IA stores a copy in every Availability Zone so a zone loss cannot lose the object
choices.why: This is wrong. One Zone-IA is a single zone. Zone loss can lose the object.

choices.text: An unattached EBS volume can still be billed
choices.why: This is true. Detach does not end the storage charge.

choices.text: A lower per-GB infrequent class can still cost more for tiny objects
choices.why: This is true when minimum size, duration, or requests dominate.

choices.text: Buying a larger database instance without measuring the workload can miss the real bottleneck
choices.why: This is true. The limit might be queries or connections, not the instance size.

spotWrong.detail: Interface endpoints are not free of hourly charges. Gateway endpoints, Spot interruption, and cache cost are described correctly.
spotWrong.hook: Interface endpoints have an hourly charge.

choices.text: An interface endpoint has no hourly charge and no data-processing charge
choices.why: This is wrong. Interface endpoints can charge hourly and for data processed.

choices.text: An S3 gateway endpoint is a route-table target without an hourly fee
choices.why: This is true for the S3 and DynamoDB gateway endpoints.

choices.text: Spot capacity can be taken back
choices.why: This is true. The instance can be interrupted.

choices.text: A cache added to cut database reads has its own cost
choices.why: This is true. The comparison includes the cache.

spotWrong.detail: An unmeasured workload is not automatically a Savings Plan. Rightsizing, One Zone-IA, and NAT versus gateway are described correctly.

choices.text: Buy a three-year commitment before any usage has been measured, because the discount cannot be wasted
choices.why: This is wrong. A commitment you do not use is wasted spend. Measure the baseline first.

choices.text: An oversized instance still costs more after you attach a discount to it
choices.why: This is true. Rightsizing removes capacity you do not need.

choices.text: One Zone-IA is appropriate when losing one Availability Zone is acceptable
choices.why: This is true only for data you can recreate or do not need after a zone loss.

choices.text: Eligible S3 traffic can avoid NAT processing by using a gateway endpoint
choices.why: This is true. The gateway endpoint takes that traffic off the NAT path.

spotWrong.detail: A cheaper engine that cannot run the workload does not meet the requirement. EBS waste, gateway pricing, and On-Demand are described correctly.
spotWrong.hook: Wrong engine is not a saving.

choices.text: Pick the database with the lowest instance price even when it cannot run the required queries
choices.why: This is wrong. The design has to meet the data requirement before the price comparison matters.

choices.text: Deleting an unused EBS volume stops its storage charge
choices.why: This is true once the volume, and not a snapshot you still need, is gone.

choices.text: An S3 gateway endpoint avoids the interface endpoint hourly fee
choices.why: This is true. The gateway endpoint has no hourly fee.

choices.text: On-Demand fits work that cannot be interrupted and has no commitment yet
choices.why: This is true. There is no term and no Spot interruption.

spotWrong.detail: Detaching a volume does not make it free. Standard-IA, Spot, and including the cache are described correctly.

choices.text: Detaching an EBS volume from every instance makes the volume free
choices.why: This is wrong. The unattached volume remains billable storage.

choices.text: Standard-IA is still stored in multiple Availability Zones
choices.why: This is true. It is the multi-AZ infrequent class.

choices.text: Spot is a fit only when the work can be interrupted and restarted
choices.why: This is true. Interruption is part of the Spot contract.

choices.text: The price of a cache belongs in the comparison that claims the cache saves money
choices.why: This is true. Savings are what remains after the cache cost.
